meta.title: General provisions and basic terms
meta.summary: You will learn how the Rules define key concepts: the parts of the road, intersection, main road, stopping and parking, overtaking and passing, types of visibility and types of vehicles, and what every road user is obliged to do. Most theory test questions are built on these terms.

p: The Road Traffic Rules of the Republic of Kazakhstan establish a uniform procedure for road traffic throughout Kazakhstan ⟦19⟧. Traffic in Kazakhstan keeps to the right ⟦20⟧.

Traffic management may be changed only by means of road signs, road markings, traffic lights, traffic controllers and orders of authorised persons. Changes are announced through the mass media, and temporary signs on a yellow background are put up at road works and where the direction of traffic is temporarily changed ⟦21⟧.
The main principle: when exercising your rights, you must not infringe the rights of others ⟦22⟧. Anyone who breaks the Rules is liable under the legislation of Kazakhstan ⟦23⟧.
lesson.tip: Almost every test question has a term hidden in it. If you know its exact meaning, you have already found half of the answer.

lesson.h: What every road user must do
p: These duties are common to drivers, pedestrians and passengers ⟦24⟧:
list: know and follow the Rules and the Road Traffic Act;
comply with the requirements of traffic controllers, traffic lights, road signs, road markings, signals at road works and the special signals of emergency and special services;
create safe conditions for traffic, act in good faith and courteously, and not cause harm to other road users or their property;
not damage or dirty the road surface, not remove, obscure or damage road signs, and not put up road signs, traffic lights or other traffic management devices without authorisation;
not throw or leave on the road any objects, materials or rubbish that obstruct traffic or are dangerous;
on finding or creating an obstruction on the road, remove it, or if that is impossible, mark it and report it to the authorised body or the road owners.
lesson.tip: A home-made “No parking” sign by the entrance to a block of flats is a violation: putting up signs without authorisation is prohibited.

lesson.h: Who counts as a road user
p: A road user is a pedestrian, a passenger or a driver ⟦25⟧.
list: A driver is a person who drives a vehicle. A drover leading livestock or pack, draught or saddle animals along a road is also a driver. A driving instructor giving a lesson is treated as a driver ⟦26⟧.

A pedestrian is a person on the road outside a vehicle who is not doing any work on it ⟦27⟧: a worker repairing the road surface is not a pedestrian. People in wheelchairs are treated as pedestrians, as are those pushing a bicycle, e-scooter, small electric vehicle, moped or motorcycle, or pulling or pushing a sledge, handcart or pram.
A passenger is a person who is in or on a vehicle but is not driving it ⟦28⟧.
lesson.tip: Pushing a bicycle or motorcycle beside you? You are a pedestrian. Got on and set off? Now you are a cyclist or a driver.

p: A road is the entire strip of land allocated for it, or the surface of a man-made structure, used for the movement of vehicles and pedestrians ⟦29⟧. It includes carriageways, tram tracks, pavements, shoulders and central reservations. Yards and car parks by shops are adjacent areas; they are not part of the road.
list: The carriageway is the part of the road intended for vehicle traffic ⟦30⟧.
A traffic lane is a longitudinal strip of the carriageway wide enough for one line of motor cars. It may or may not be marked with road markings ⟦31⟧.

The edge of the carriageway is defined by road markings or, if there are none, by the edge of the road surface. If the edge of the surface cannot be made out, road users determine the edge themselves by the edge of the worn track ⟦32⟧.
The shoulder adjoins the carriageway but is not part of it. It is needed for the stability of the road, for safety, for pedestrians and cyclists, and in case of emergencies ⟦33⟧.
The pavement is the part of the road for pedestrians that adjoins the carriageway or is separated from it by a lawn ⟦34⟧.

The central reservation (dividing strip) is a structurally separate element between adjacent carriageways. It is not intended for non-rail vehicles or pedestrians to move or stop on; the exception is a forced stop by pedestrians crossing the road outside a built-up area ⟦35⟧. If there is only a double solid line instead of a central reservation, there is just one carriageway.
lesson.tip: No markings, but wide enough for two lines of vehicles? There are still lanes: drivers determine their number themselves from the width of the carriageway and the dimensions of the vehicles ⟦36⟧.

p: An intersection is a place where roads cross, join or branch at the same level ⟦37⟧. Its boundaries are imaginary lines connecting the opposite starting points of the carriageway corner curves that are farthest from the centre of the intersection.
Exits from adjacent areas are not intersections. Nor are places where field and forest tracks join a road.
An adjacent area is an area directly adjoining the road that is not intended for through traffic ⟦38⟧. An example is a shopping centre car park. The Rules must be followed there too.
lesson.tip: An exit from a car park or a yard onto a street looks like a side road joining it, but it is not an intersection.

p: A main road is a road marked with signs 2.1, 2.3.1-2.3.3 or 5.1 in relation to the road it crosses or that joins it. A paved road (asphalt, concrete, stone materials) is also a main road in relation to a dirt road ⟦39⟧.
An important caveat: if a minor road has a paved section immediately before the intersection, this does not make it equal in status to the road it crosses ⟦40⟧.
Priority (right of way) is the right to move first in the intended direction in relation to other road users ⟦41⟧.
To give way (not impede) means not to move off, resume or continue moving and not to make a manoeuvre if this would force a road user who has priority to change direction or speed ⟦42⟧.
lesson.tip: If a driver with priority had to slow down or swerve because of you, you did not give way, even if there was no collision.

p: If you are stationary because traffic management requires it (for example, at a red traffic light), this is neither stopping nor parking ⟦43⟧.
list: Stopping is an intentional halt of up to 5 minutes. A longer halt is also stopping if the time is needed for passengers to board or alight, or for loading or unloading ⟦44⟧.
Parking is an intentional halt of more than 5 minutes for reasons not related to passengers boarding or alighting, loading or unloading ⟦45⟧.
A forced stop is a halt caused by a technical fault, a hazard from the load being carried, the condition of the driver or a passenger, or an obstruction appearing on the road ⟦46⟧.
lesson.tip: The difference is not only the time but also the purpose: letting a passenger out or unloading can take as long as needed, and it is still stopping.

p: Every overtaking manoeuvre is passing, but not all passing is overtaking. If you simply drive in your own lane faster than the next lane, that is passing. If you move into the adjacent lane and stay there, that is changing lanes, not overtaking.

Driving around a stationary vehicle is not overtaking: only moving vehicles are overtaken. The Rules define manoeuvring as moving off, stopping, turning and making a U-turn, changing lanes, braking and reversing ⟦47⟧.
list: Passing is moving faster than a vehicle in the adjacent lane travelling in the same direction ⟦48⟧.
Overtaking is passing one or more vehicles by leaving the lane you occupy and then returning to that lane ⟦49⟧.
Changing lanes is moving from one traffic lane to another while keeping the original direction of travel ⟦50⟧.
lesson.tip: The overtaking formula: leave your lane, pass, return to your original lane.

list: Poor visibility: visibility of the road of less than 300 m in fog, rain, snowfall, dust and at twilight ⟦51⟧. The cause is the weather or twilight.

Restricted view: the driver can see the road in the direction of travel for less than 100 m because the view is blocked by the terrain, bends in the road, vegetation, buildings, structures or other objects, including vehicles ⟦52⟧.
Hours of darkness: the period from the end of evening twilight to the beginning of morning twilight ⟦53⟧.
lesson.tip: Fog and snowfall mean “poor visibility” (less than 300 m). Bushes on a bend or a rise in the road mean a “restricted view” (less than 100 m).

list: A traffic hazard is a situation in which continuing to move in the same direction at the same speed creates a risk of a road traffic accident ⟦54⟧.

An obstruction is a stationary object in a traffic lane that makes it impossible to continue in that lane ⟦55⟧. A traffic jam, or a vehicle that has stopped in the lane in accordance with the Rules, is not an obstruction.

lesson.h: Built-up area, residential zone and motorway
list: A built-up area is a developed area whose entrances and exits are marked with signs 5.22-5.25 ⟦56⟧. The requirements for built-up areas apply from sign 5.22 to sign 5.23, not from the first house to the last. The blue sign 5.24 shows the name of the place, but the requirements for built-up areas do not apply on that road.
A residential zone is a site, developed area or housing estate marked with sign 5.38 ⟦57⟧. Without the sign, an area is not a residential zone.

A motorway is marked with sign 5.1. It has separate carriageways with a central reservation and no crossings at the same level, and it can be entered only from other roads via grade-separated interchanges: it does not serve roadside properties ⟦58⟧.
A motor car is a motor vehicle for carrying people, goods or equipment; trolleybuses are included. Tractors and self-propelled machines are not motor cars ⟦59⟧.
A motor vehicle is a self-propelled vehicle with an engine. Tractors fall under this term, but e-scooters, small electric vehicles and rail vehicles (trams) do not ⟦60⟧.
A bus has more than 8 seats, not counting the driver's seat ⟦61⟧.

A road train (vehicle combination) is a motor vehicle coupled to one or more trailers; a semi-trailer also counts as a trailer ⟦62⟧. The maximum authorised mass of a road train is the sum of the maximum authorised masses of all its units ⟦63⟧.

A moped is a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with an internal combustion engine of up to 50 cm³ or an electric motor and a maximum design speed of no more than 50 km/h; scooters and mokicks with the same characteristics count as mopeds ⟦64⟧. A motorcycle is a two-wheeled motor vehicle; three- and four-wheeled vehicles with an unladen mass of up to 400 kg and scooters over 50 cm³ count as motorcycles ⟦65⟧.

An e-scooter has 2-3 wheels and no seat, carries one person and has a top speed of no more than 25 km/h ⟦66⟧. A bicycle has two or more wheels and is propelled by the muscle power of the people on it, including with the help of a motor ⟦67⟧.
A route vehicle is a public bus, trolleybus or tram running on a route with designated stops ⟦68⟧. Public transport is a wider term: it also includes taxis ⟦69⟧.
lesson.tip: A passenger car with a trailer is also a road train.

lesson.h: A few more terms for the test
list: A traffic controller is not only a police officer: the role can also be performed by a military police officer, a member of a military traffic control unit, a transport control officer, a road maintenance worker, or an attendant at a level crossing or ferry crossing, provided they have the proper ID and equipment ⟦70⟧.
A level crossing is where a road crosses railway tracks at the same level. Its boundary is an imaginary line 10 m from the nearest rail ⟦71⟧.
A pedestrian crossing is marked with signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and/or road markings. Without markings, its width is the distance between signs 5.16.1 and 5.16.2 along the centre line of the road ⟦72⟧.

An organised convoy is at least three motor vehicles travelling one behind the other in the same lane with their headlights on at all times, escorted by a lead vehicle with a flashing blue (or blue and red) beacon ⟦73⟧.
A road traffic accident is an event that occurs while a vehicle is moving on a road and involves that vehicle, resulting in injury, death or material damage ⟦74⟧.
A retroreflective item must make a person visible from 150 m in dipped headlights and from 400 m in main-beam headlights ⟦75⟧.

keyFacts: A main road is marked with signs 2.1, 2.3.1-2.3.3 or 5.1; a paved road is the main road in relation to a dirt road ⟦2⟧.
A paved section on a minor road before an intersection does not make it equal to the road it crosses ⟦3⟧.
Stopping: up to 5 minutes, or longer for boarding, alighting, loading or unloading; parking: more than 5 minutes for other reasons ⟦4⟧.
A halt required by traffic management (for example, by a red light) counts as neither stopping nor parking ⟦5⟧.
Overtaking is passing that involves leaving your lane and returning to the lane you were in before ⟦6⟧.
Poor visibility: less than 300 m in fog, rain, snowfall, dust and at twilight ⟦7⟧.
Restricted view: less than 100 m in the direction of travel because of terrain, bends in the road, vegetation, buildings and other objects ⟦8⟧.
Exits from adjacent areas are not intersections ⟦9⟧.
A built-up area is marked with signs 5.22-5.25, a residential zone with sign 5.38 ⟦10⟧.
A traffic lane does not have to be marked with road markings ⟦11⟧.
A bus has more than 8 seats, not counting the driver's seat ⟦12⟧.
mistakes: Thinking that any halt longer than 5 minutes is parking. If you spend 20 minutes unloading the boot, it is stopping ⟦13⟧.
Confusing overtaking and passing. Driving in your own lane faster than the next lane is passing; overtaking always involves leaving your lane ⟦14⟧.
Thinking that an asphalt section before an intersection makes a dirt road equal to an asphalt road. It does not ⟦15⟧.
Confusing poor visibility with a restricted view. Poor visibility is caused by weather and twilight (less than 300 m), a restricted view by terrain and objects (less than 100 m) ⟦16⟧.
Treating an exit from a car park or a yard as an intersection. Exits from adjacent areas are not intersections ⟦17⟧.
Thinking that lanes exist only where road markings are painted. A traffic lane can exist without markings ⟦18⟧.

questions.q: You are driving on a dirt road and approaching an intersection with an asphalt road. There are no priority signs. Which road is the main road?
options: The dirt road you are driving on
They are of equal status, as there are no signs
questions.explain: You are on a dirt road, and a paved road (asphalt, concrete, stone materials) is the main road in relation to a dirt road. So the asphalt road is the main road here.

questions.q: You are driving on a dirt road. Shortly before the intersection with an asphalt road, a short asphalt section begins. There are no signs. Which road is the main road?
options: The roads are now of equal status, as both are paved
Your road, as you are already driving on asphalt
The asphalt road; yours remains the minor road
questions.explain: Your road is a dirt road, and a short stretch of asphalt before the intersection does not change that. A paved section on a minor road immediately before an intersection does not make it equal in status to the road it crosses.

questions.q: You leave your car outside a shop and go shopping for 15 minutes. There are no passengers or goods. What is this called under the Rules?
questions.explain: You are away for more than 5 minutes, nobody is getting in or out and nothing is being loaded. Parking is an intentional halt of more than 5 minutes for reasons not related to passengers boarding or alighting, loading or unloading.

questions.q: You spend 20 minutes unloading heavy boxes from the boot at the edge of the carriageway. What is this called under the Rules?
options: Parking, because it has lasted more than 5 minutes
Stopping, because the time is needed for unloading
questions.explain: You are stationary for more than 5 minutes, but the time is needed for unloading. Stopping is a halt of up to 5 minutes, or longer if the time is needed for passengers to board or alight, or for loading or unloading.

questions.q: You are waiting at a red traffic light before an intersection. How do the Rules classify this halt?
options: It is parking if you wait longer than 5 minutes
It counts as neither stopping nor parking
questions.explain: You are stationary because the traffic light requires it. A halt required by traffic management does not count as stopping (parking).

questions.q: Your engine has stalled on the way, the car will not start, and you are stationary at the edge of the road. What is this called?
questions.explain: The car is stationary because of a technical fault. A forced stop is a halt caused by a fault, a hazard from the load, the condition of the driver (passenger) or an obstruction on the road.

questions.q: You are driving in the left lane of a multi-lane road faster than the vehicles in the right lane, and you do not change lanes. What is this called under the Rules?
questions.explain: Passing is moving at a higher speed than a vehicle in the adjacent lane travelling in the same direction. You do not leave your lane, so this is not overtaking.

questions.q: Which of these manoeuvres counts as overtaking under the Rules?
options: You drive in your lane faster than a bus in the next lane
You pass a truck by leaving your lane, then return to it
You move into the next lane so as to turn from it later
You drive around a pothole in your lane, passing no one
questions.explain: Overtaking is passing one or more vehicles by leaving the lane you occupy and then returning to that lane.

questions.q: In the morning there is thick fog, and you can see the road for about 200 m. What do the Rules call these conditions?
options: Normal visibility, as the road is visible beyond 100 m
questions.explain: Because of the fog, the road is visible for less than 300 m. Poor visibility means visibility of the road of less than 300 m in fog, rain, snowfall, dust and at twilight.

questions.q: It is a clear day. The road bends, bushes block the view, and you can see the road ahead for about 70 m. What is this kind of visibility called?
questions.explain: Your view is limited to less than 100 m by the bushes on the bend, not by the weather. A restricted view means that the road is visible for less than 100 m in the direction of travel because of terrain, bends in the road, vegetation, buildings or other objects.

questions.q: You pulled out of a minor road onto a main road, and a driver on the main road had to slow down because of you. Did you comply with the requirement to “give way”?
options: Yes, because there was no collision
Yes, if you switched on your direction indicator in advance
No: you forced the driver with priority to change speed
It depends on whether you got up to their speed in time
questions.explain: To give way means not to move off or continue moving if this would force a road user with priority to change direction or speed.

questions.q: You are leaving a shopping centre car park, which is not intended for through traffic, and driving onto a street. Is the exit point an intersection?
options: No, it is an exit from an adjacent area
Yes, it is where roads join at the same level
Yes, if the exit is wide and has an asphalt surface
questions.explain: Such a car park is an adjacent area, and exits from adjacent areas are not intersections.

questions.q: A man is walking along the shoulder, pushing a bicycle beside him. How do the Rules classify him?
questions.explain: The man is not riding but pushing the bicycle beside him. People pushing a bicycle, e-scooter, moped or motorcycle are treated as pedestrians.

questions.q: The road has no markings, but it is wide enough for vehicles travelling in one direction to drive in two lines. Does it have traffic lanes?
options: Yes, a traffic lane may exist without road markings
No, lanes exist only where there are road markings
No, without markings the whole carriageway counts as one lane
questions.explain: A traffic lane is a longitudinal strip of the carriageway wide enough for one line of motor cars, whether or not it is marked. Without markings, drivers determine the number of lanes themselves, taking into account the width of the carriageway, the dimensions of the vehicles and the clearance between them.

questions.q: You have just driven past the sign shown in the diagram. There are no houses around yet; the buildings start further on. Do the requirements of the Rules for driving in built-up areas apply to you?
options: Yes, from where this sign is placed
No, only from the first houses
No, not until you reach a speed limit sign
Only during the hours of darkness
questions.explain: You have driven past sign 5.22 “Start of built-up area”. Under the Rules, a built-up area is defined by signs 5.22-5.25, not by buildings, so its requirements apply from the point where the sign is placed.

questions.q: You have just driven past the sign shown in the diagram, but there are still houses along the road. Do the requirements of the Rules for driving in built-up areas apply to you?
options: Yes, as long as there are still houses along the road
Yes, up to the first intersection after the sign
No, they stop applying at this sign
questions.explain: This is sign 5.23 “End of built-up area”. From the point where it is placed, the requirements for built-up areas stop applying on this road, even if the houses continue.

questions.q: You are approaching an asphalt road along a dirt road and want to turn left. There are no signs. Who must give way?
options: You must give way to the blue car
The blue car must give way to you: you are on its right
questions.explain: You are on a dirt road, and a paved road is the main road in relation to a dirt road. So you let the blue car go first, even though it is approaching from the left: the “priority to the right” rule applies only on roads of equal status.

questions.q: You are driving straight on along an asphalt road. A blue car is approaching from the right along a dirt road and is turning left. There are no signs. Who must give way?
options: You must give way to the blue car: it is on your right
The blue car must give way to you
questions.explain: The blue car is coming out of a dirt road, which is a minor road in relation to the asphalt road. So it must give way to you, even though it is on your right.

questions.q: A red car is leaving the yard of a block of flats onto the street. What do the Rules call such a yard, and do the Rules apply in it?
options: An adjacent area; the Rules do not apply there
A minor road; the Rules apply there
A residential zone; the Rules do not apply there
An adjacent area; the Rules apply there
questions.explain: The yard adjoins the road and is not intended for through traffic, so it is an adjacent area. The Rules state explicitly that traffic in an adjacent area is subject to the Rules.

questions.q: How many carriageways does the road in the diagram have?
questions.explain: There is a central reservation in the middle of the road. It separates adjacent carriageways, so there are two carriageways here, each with two traffic lanes.

questions.q: How many carriageways does the road in the diagram have?
questions.explain: The double solid line is a road marking, not a central reservation: there is no structurally separate element here. So there is one carriageway, and it has four traffic lanes.

questions.q: A box that fell off a truck is lying in the right lane, and there is a traffic jam in the left lane. Which of these do the Rules call an obstruction to traffic?
options: Only the box in the right lane
Only the traffic jam in the left lane
Both the box and the traffic jam
questions.explain: An obstruction is a stationary object in a lane that makes it impossible to continue in that lane: that is the box. The Rules explicitly exclude a traffic jam, as well as a vehicle that has stopped in the lane in accordance with the Rules.

questions.q: The driver of the blue car has pulled over onto the shoulder and switched on the hazard warning lights because a passenger suddenly felt unwell. What is this halt called?
questions.explain: The car has halted because of the passenger's condition. This is a forced stop: that is what the Rules call a halt caused by a fault, a hazard from the load, the condition of the driver or a passenger, or an obstruction on the road.

questions.q: The driver of the blue car spends 12 minutes loading shopping into the boot. The driver of the white car sits in the car for 12 minutes waiting for a friend; nobody gets in or out. Which of them is parking under the Rules?
questions.explain: The blue car's driver is loading, so this is stopping, however long it lasts. The white car has been stationary for more than 5 minutes with no boarding, alighting, loading or unloading: that is parking.

questions.q: It is a clear day. You are driving behind a truck that blocks your view: you can see the road ahead for about 40 m. What do the Rules call this kind of visibility?
options: Normal visibility: only terrain and buildings can restrict it
questions.explain: The weather is clear, but the truck limits your view to less than 100 m. A restricted view is a view of less than 100 m in the direction of travel because of terrain, bends in the road, vegetation, buildings or other objects, including vehicles.

questions.q: It is midnight. The street is well lit by street lights, and you can see the road far ahead. Does this count as the hours of darkness under the Rules?
options: No, as the street is well lit
No, if the road is visible beyond 300 m
questions.explain: The hours of darkness are the period from the end of evening twilight to the beginning of morning twilight. Street lights do not change the time of day, so midnight falls within the hours of darkness even on a lit street.

questions.q: The driver of the red car is driving around the blue car, which has broken down and is standing in the lane with its hazard warning lights on. Is this manoeuvre overtaking?
options: Yes, as the red car moves into the oncoming lane
Yes, if the blue car has stood there for less than 5 minutes
No: only passing a truck counts as overtaking
No, this is driving around a stationary car
questions.explain: The blue car is stationary, so the red car is driving around it, not overtaking it. Overtaking is passing a moving vehicle ahead by leaving your lane and then returning to it.

questions.q: Which vehicles in the diagram are road trains?
options: Only the tractor unit with a semi-trailer
Only the passenger car with a trailer
questions.explain: A road train is a motor vehicle coupled to one or more trailers. A passenger car with a trailer is also a road train, and the term “trailer” also covers semi-trailers.

questions.q: The red car has stopped 5 m from the nearest rail (see the diagram). Is it within the boundaries of the level crossing?
options: Yes: the crossing boundary is 10 m from the rail
No: the crossing begins only at the rails themselves
No, if the barrier is raised
Yes, but only when a train is approaching the crossing
questions.explain: The boundary of a level crossing is an imaginary line 10 m from the nearest rail. The car is 5 m from the rail, so it is already within the level crossing.

questions.q: Three cars with their headlights on are driving one behind the other in the same lane. A police car with its flashing beacons on is escorting them at the front. What do the Rules call such a group?
questions.explain: An organised convoy is a group of three or more motor vehicles travelling one behind the other in the same lane with their headlights on at all times, escorted by a lead vehicle with a flashing blue (or blue and red) beacon.

questions.q: You are driving on a dirt road with no markings, and the edge of the surface cannot be made out. How is the edge of the carriageway determined?
options: By the line of the nearest road signs
By the road user, from the edge of the worn track
The middle of the dirt road is considered the edge
There is no carriageway edge on a dirt road
questions.explain: The edge of the carriageway is defined by road markings or, if there are none, by the edge of the road surface. If it is impossible to identify the edge of the surface, road users determine the edge themselves by the edge of the worn track.

questions.q: You have entered a road with sign 5.1 “Motorway”. Which feature does NOT fit the definition of a motorway in the Rules?
options: You can drive onto it directly from a yard or a roadside property
The carriageways for each direction are separated by a central reservation
It does not cross roads, railway or tram tracks at the same level
It can be entered only from other roads via grade-separated interchanges
questions.explain: A motorway does not serve roadside properties: you can get onto it only from other roads via grade-separated interchanges. It has separate carriageways with a central reservation and no crossings at the same level.

questions.q: On which path will the red car overtake the truck?
questions.explain: On path A the car leaves its lane, passes the truck and returns to its original lane: this is overtaking. On path B it only changes lanes and stays in the left lane, and without a return to the original lane there is no overtaking.

questions.q: There are no markings, but the carriageway is wide enough for two lines of traffic. On which path will the red car change lanes?
options: Neither path: there are no lanes without markings
questions.explain: A traffic lane does not have to be marked: if the width allows two lines of traffic, there are two lanes. Moving into the adjacent line on path B is changing lanes, while on path A the car stays in its lane.

questions.q: On which path will you be turning at an intersection?
questions.explain: On the right, a road joins the street: this is an intersection. On the left is an entrance to a yard, that is, to an adjacent area, and exits from adjacent areas (and entrances to them) are not intersections.

questions.q: On the left, a field track joins the highway; on the right is the entrance to a filling station. On which path will you be turning at an intersection?
questions.explain: Neither of these places is an intersection. Places where field and forest tracks join a road are not intersections, and neither are exits from adjacent areas (and entrances to them), such as a filling station.

questions.q: A road outside a built-up area. The blue car has pulled onto the shoulder, and the white car is standing at the right-hand edge of the asphalt. Which of them is on the carriageway?
questions.explain: There is no edge marking line, so the edge of the carriageway is the edge of the asphalt, and the white car is on the carriageway. The blue car is on the shoulder: the shoulder adjoins the carriageway but is not part of it.

questions.q: Which of the actions shown do the Rules classify as manoeuvring?
options: A only: stopping at the edge
questions.explain: Manoeuvring means moving off from a standstill, stopping, turning and making a U-turn, changing lanes, braking and reversing. So both stopping at the edge (A) and changing lanes (B) are manoeuvres.

questions.q: A vehicle has 8 seats, not counting the driver's seat. Is it a bus as defined by the Rules?
options: Yes, as it has more than five seats
Yes, if it carries passengers for payment
No: a bus needs more than eight seats besides the driver's
No: only a vehicle with two passenger doors is classed as a bus
questions.explain: A bus is a motor car for carrying passengers and luggage that has more than eight seats, not including the driver's seat. Eight seats are not enough.

questions.q: Which of the following do the Rules classify as a motor car?
options: A self-propelled machine, such as a loader
questions.explain: A motor car is a motor vehicle for carrying people, goods or equipment, including trolleybuses. Tractors and self-propelled machines are not motor cars, and a tram is a rail vehicle.

questions.q: Which of these vehicles is NOT a motor vehicle as defined by the Rules?
questions.explain: A motor vehicle is a self-propelled road vehicle with an engine. The exceptions are named explicitly: e-scooters, small electric vehicles and rail vehicles, which include trams. Tractors, on the other hand, are included in the term.

questions.q: Which vehicle do the Rules call an e-scooter?
options: Any two- or three-wheeled vehicle with an electric motor
With a seat, for one person, no faster than 50 km/h
Any electric unicycle or hoverboard for one person
Two or three wheels, no seat, no faster than 25 km/h
questions.explain: An e-scooter is a personal mobility device with two or three wheels for one person, without a seat, with a maximum design speed of no more than 25 km/h. It is not a motor vehicle.

questions.q: A scooter has a 50 cm³ engine and a maximum design speed of 45 km/h. Which category of vehicles does it belong to under the Rules?
questions.explain: A moped is a two- or three-wheeled motor vehicle with an internal combustion engine of no more than 50 cm³ (or an electric motor) and a speed of no more than 50 km/h. Scooters with these characteristics are explicitly treated as mopeds.

questions.q: A three-wheeled vehicle with a 250 cm³ engine has an unladen mass of 380 kg. What do the Rules treat it as?
questions.explain: The engine is larger than 50 cm³, so it is not a moped. Three- and four-wheeled vehicles with an unladen mass of no more than 400 kg are treated as motorcycles, and 380 kg is within this limit.

questions.q: The maximum authorised mass of a car is 2000 kg, and that of its trailer is 750 kg. What is the maximum authorised mass of this road train?
questions.explain: The maximum authorised mass of a vehicle combination is the sum of the maximum authorised masses of all the vehicles in it: 2000 + 750 = 2750 kg.

questions.q: Which of these people can act as a traffic controller?
options: A driver who was first to arrive at an accident scene and stepped into the road
A security guard from a nearby shop with a whistle and a torch
A road maintenance worker with an ID card and a baton
Any adult pedestrian in a reflective vest
questions.explain: A traffic controller can be not only a police officer but also, for example, a road maintenance worker or an attendant at a level crossing or ferry crossing. The condition is the appropriate ID and equipment (a uniform or armband, a baton, a disc with a red signal, a red lamp or a flag).

questions.q: Which vehicle is a route vehicle as defined by the Rules?
options: A taxi carrying a passenger on a booked trip
A truck delivering goods to shops
The private car you use to drive to work
A tram running on its route
questions.explain: A route vehicle is a public bus, trolleybus or tram carrying passengers on an established route with designated stops. A taxi is also public transport, but it is not a route vehicle.

questions.q: Which of these events is a road traffic accident?
options: A moving car hit and damaged a barrier
A tree branch fell on a parked car
A pedestrian slipped and fell on the pavement by the road
A driver broke the key in the ignition in a car park
questions.explain: A road traffic accident is an event that occurs while a vehicle is moving on a road and involves that vehicle, resulting in injury, death, damage to vehicles, structures or goods, or other material damage. A barrier damaged by a moving car fits this definition; the other cases do not.

questions.q: A pedestrian is wearing a retroreflective item at night. From what distance must this item make the pedestrian visible in dipped headlights?
questions.explain: A retroreflective item reflects headlight beams back towards their source and ensures visibility from 150 m with dipped headlights and from 400 m with main-beam headlights.

questions.q: Which of these people is NOT considered a pedestrian?
options: A person pushing a moped beside them
A worker repairing the road surface
questions.explain: A pedestrian is a person on the road outside a vehicle who is not doing any work on it. So a worker repairing the surface is not a pedestrian. The Rules treat people in wheelchairs and those pushing a moped or a pram as pedestrians.

questions.q: Which of these people is a passenger?
options: A person on the rear seat of a motorcycle
A person pushing a motorcycle beside them
A driving instructor during a lesson
A drover leading horses along the road
questions.explain: A passenger is a person who is on or in a vehicle and is not driving it. A person pushing a motorcycle is treated as a pedestrian, while a driving instructor and a drover are treated as drivers.

questions.q: A man is herding a flock of sheep along the road. How do the Rules classify him?
questions.explain: A driver is not only a person who drives a vehicle. A drover leading livestock or pack, draught or saddle animals along a road is also considered a driver.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the road?
questions.explain: A road includes carriageways and, where they exist, tram tracks, pavements, shoulders and central reservations. A yard is an adjacent area: it only adjoins the road.

questions.q: How is the width of a pedestrian crossing determined if it has no road markings?
options: By the width of the pavements on both sides of the road
It is always taken as 4 m along the centre line of the road
By the distance between signs 5.16.1 and 5.16.2
There is no pedestrian crossing without road markings
questions.explain: A pedestrian crossing is marked with signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and/or road markings. If there are no markings, its width is determined by the distance between signs 5.16.1 and 5.16.2 along the centre line of the road.

questions.q: When is a pedestrian allowed to stop on a central reservation?
options: When forced to stop outside a built-up area
Never: a central reservation is not for pedestrians
Anywhere, if there are no vehicles nearby
Only in a built-up area, next to a pedestrian crossing
questions.explain: A central reservation is not intended for non-rail vehicles or pedestrians to move or stop on. The only exception is a forced stop by pedestrians crossing the road outside a built-up area.

questions.q: You are approaching an intersection with an asphalt road along a dirt road. There are no signs. On which path may you move off before the blue car?
questions.explain: The asphalt road is the main road in relation to the dirt road, so you must let the blue car go first whichever way you are going. Going straight on (A), you would cross its path, and turning right (B), you would pull out right in front of it into its lane.

questions.q: Under the Rules, what makes an area a residential zone?
questions.explain: A residential zone is a site, developed area or housing estate marked with sign 5.38. Without this sign, an area is not a residential zone, even if there are residential buildings all around.

questions.q: Which type of traffic is established for vehicles in Kazakhstan?
options: Left-hand on motorways, right-hand on other roads
questions.explain: Right-hand traffic is established for vehicles throughout the Republic of Kazakhstan.

questions.q: Temporary road signs have been put up at a road works site. What background do they have?
questions.explain: At road works and where the direction of traffic is temporarily changed, temporary road signs on a yellow background are used. Traffic management may be changed only by road signs, road markings, traffic lights, traffic controllers and orders of authorised persons.

questions.q: You notice a large branch lying on the carriageway: it has fallen from a tree. What do the Rules require of a road user in this situation?
options: Nothing: clearing the road is only the road services' job
Drive around it and carry on without telling anyone
Report it only if someone has already damaged a car on it
Remove it or, if you cannot, mark it and report it
questions.explain: On finding an obstruction on the road, a road user must take steps to remove it. If it cannot be removed, the obstruction must be marked and reported to the authorised road safety body or to the road owners.

questions.q: A resident has put up a home-made “No parking” sign by the entrance to their block of flats so that nobody parks there. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, if the sign looks like a real one
No, signs may not be put up without authorisation
Yes, residents may do so by their own entrance
Yes, if the sign is temporary and on a yellow background
questions.explain: Road users must not put up road signs, traffic lights or other traffic management devices without authorisation, or remove, obscure or damage signs.
